text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD

- Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel admits in parliament that there was pressure from the Iranian government in the affair surrounding the release of the alleged murderers of three Kurdish leaders in Vienna in 1989. The government rejected opposition demands for a parliamentary investigation into the affair.
- The introduction of Europe's single currency will push up interest rates, says communal financing bank Kommunalkredit.
- Liberal and Green opposition parties, supported by christian and humanitarian organisations, criticise the government's newly reformed immigration laws as too strict.
- All parties in Vienna's municipal parliament except the ruling Social Democrats want the City of Vienna's stake in Bank Austria to be sold as soon as possible.
- Austria's municipalities are expected to have no problems meeting the Maastricht criteria for Europe's single currency, as they can exlcude up to half of all relevant deficits.
- Bank Austria, Tele Danmark, and UTA, the telecoms company set up by Austria's regional energy providers, said they will make a joint bid for Austria's third mobile phone licence.
- Austria resists abolishing its anonymous saviongs accounts as demanded by the European Union, saying such a step would damage the country's capital markets.
- Austria's unemployment rate rose to 4.4 percent in April from 4.1 percent in March.
- Increased electricity prices raised national grid company Verbund's turnover in 1996 even though electricity sales were down. Pre-tax profit rose to 1.52 billion schillings from 1.41 billion.
- Die Erste savings bank wants to take the lead in Austria's savings bank sector by taking over GiroCredit.
- Postal savings bank PSK will be transformed into a joint stock company today. Its sole owner, state holding PTBG, plans to sell a 49-percent stake before the summer.
- Microchip maker AMS will reduce its 1996 dividend to ten schillings from 12 schillings the year before.
DIE PRESSE
- Austrians paid one fifth more taxes in the first four months of the current year than in the same period a year ago.
- Austrian Energy, a unit of engineering group VA Technologie, received a 287 million schillings order to build a coal power station in Mongolia.
- The coalition government has agreed to start selling its stake in Bank Austria before the end of the year, but experts doubt a speedy sale will be possible.
- Conservative Economics Minister Hannes Farnleitner wants more competition in Austria's new draft telecommunications law.
- Postal savings bank PSK will be allowed for the first time to make loans to private customers.
KURIER
- Hannes Swoboda, Social Democrat Member of the European Parliament, says Austria will not be part of the first wave of countries to join NATO.
- Labour unions refuse industry's demands to create more low-pay jobs.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT

- Wolfgang Ruttenstorfer, state secretary in the finance ministry, says employment and economic growth should take precedence to a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for Europe's single currency.
